text:
1. Johnson's praise of Shakespeare rests on a single principle.
2. Johnson holds that only just representations of general nature can please many people and please them for a long time.
3. In Johnson's account, the dramatists who wrote alongside Shakespeare drew characters as shaped by the customs of a particular court or city.
4. In Johnson's account, those contemporaries' characters were fitted to the fashions of a particular season.
5. In Johnson's account, those contemporaries' characters spoke the slang of a narrow social circle and dealt with the follies of a single year.
6. In Johnson's account, when the fashions of their time passed, those contemporaries' characters lost their force.
7. A later reader finds in those contemporaries' characters only the outward trappings of a vanished time.
8. In Johnson's account, Shakespeare's characters act and speak from passions and principles common to every age and every country.
9. In Johnson's account, emotions such as a father's grief or a counsellor's vanity are the same in any place and any era.
10. Johnson does not deny that Shakespeare's plays bear the marks of their own time.
11. Johnson holds that the period-specific marks in Shakespeare's plays are only superficial.
12. Johnson holds that beneath those surface marks lies the common nature of mankind.
13. A reader who knows nothing of Elizabethan manners can still find Polonius believable.
14. The universality of Shakespeare's characters explains why such a reader can believe in Polonius.
